questions.text: What is the strength reduction factor (φ) for flexure in a reinforced concrete beam?

options.text: φ = 0.70, applicable to compression-controlled sections
φ = 0.75, typically used for sections with moderate ductility
φ = 0.85, generally for sections with high ductility demands
φ = 0.90 (tension-controlled members only, ε_t ≥ 0.005)

rationale.a: φ = 0.70 applies to tied axial compression and bearing, not flexure.
rationale.b: φ = 0.75 applies to spirally reinforced axial compression.
rationale.c: φ = 0.85 applies to shear, torsion, and post-tensioned anchorage.
rationale.correct: Flexure is a ductile failure mode; the steel reinforcement yields and elongates before the concrete crushes, providing visible warning. The highest φ factor (0.90) reflects this ductility.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: For a reinforced concrete column with rectangular tie reinforcement, what is the strength reduction factor for axial compression?

rationale.a: φ = 0.75 applies to spirally reinforced (not tied) columns.
rationale.c: φ = 0.85 applies to shear and torsion.
rationale.d: φ = 0.90 applies to flexure and tension.
rationale.correct: Tied columns have rectangular or square ties that confine the concrete core, but less effectively than spiral reinforcement. The lower φ = 0.70 reflects the reduced ductility and brittleness of this failure mode.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: Why does a spirally reinforced column receive a higher strength reduction factor (φ = 0.75) compared to a tied column (φ = 0.70)?

options.text: Spiral reinforcement is stronger in tension than tie bars, providing enhanced structural integrity
Spiral confinement prevents core concrete from bursting and provides post-peak ductility, allowing load redistribution.
Spiral columns are always taller than tied columns, so they are more stable and less prone to buckling
The NSCP arbitrarily assigns higher φ to spiral columns to encourage their use in specific applications

rationale.a: Strength of the reinforcement steel is not the governing factor; confinement is.
rationale.c: Column height and stability relate to slenderness, not the φ factor for a given failure mode.
rationale.d: Code decisions are based on structural mechanics, not arbitrary preferences.
rationale.correct: The continuous helical spiral reinforcement wraps the concrete core, preventing lateral expansion and concrete spalling. When axial load is applied, the spiral confines the core, allowing the column to sustain load even after the outer concrete cracks. This provides ductility and warning before collapse.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: Post-tensioned concrete beams have anchorage zones where stress is transferred from the tendons to the concrete. The NSCP assigns φ = 0.85 to this failure mode. Based on the φ factor hierarchy, why is it different from φ = 0.90 (flexure) and φ = 0.70 (bearing)?

options.text: Anchorage zones are purely brittle, like bearing, so they should use φ = 0.70, which is more appropriate for brittle failure modes
Anchorage zones exhibit mixed behavior: some ductility from spreading stresses in surrounding concrete, plus some local crushing. The intermediate φ = 0.85 reflects this hybrid behavior.
Post-tensioned beams are always stronger than reinforced beams, so φ = 0.85 is used to prevent over-design, ensuring safety without excessive material use
φ = 0.85 is assigned to anchorage zones to match the shear φ factor arbitrarily, without specific consideration of the actual behavior

rationale.a: Anchorage zones are not purely brittle; they benefit from stress redistribution in surrounding concrete.
rationale.c: Material strength has no bearing on the φ factor; ductility and predictability do.
rationale.d: The match to shear φ is coincidental; each φ is assigned based on failure mode characteristics.
rationale.correct: Anchorage zones involve stress transfer that is partly ductile (concrete around the anchor deforms and redistributes stress) and partly prone to local bearing failure. The intermediate φ = 0.85 reflects this hybrid nature—less conservative than pure bearing (0.70), more conservative than pure flexure (0.90).
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A reinforced concrete beam must resist a required shear force V_u = 250 kN. The nominal shear strength is V_n = 300 kN. Is the beam adequate for shear?

options.text: φVn = 0.90 × 300 = 270 kN ≥ 250 kN; adequate.
φVn = 0.85 × 300 = 255 kN ≥ 250 kN; adequate.
φVn = 0.75 × 300 = 225 kN < 250 kN; not adequate.
φVn = 0.70 × 300 = 210 kN < 250 kN; not adequate.

rationale.d: Tied compression and bearing use φ = 0.70.
rationale.correct: Shear uses φ = 0.85. Design capacity = 0.85(300) = 255 kN. Required shear = 250 kN. Since 255 ≥ 250, the beam is adequate for shear.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.explanation: Flexure uses φ = 0.90, not shear. Spiral compression uses φ = 0.75. Tied compression and bearing use φ = 0.70. Shear uses φ = 0.85. Design capacity = 0.85(300) = 255 kN. Required shear = 250 kN. Since 255 ≥ 250, the beam is adequate for shear. Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: Why is the strength reduction factor for bearing on concrete (φ = 0.70) the same as for tied column compression (φ = 0.70)?

options.text: Both are ductile failure modes that provide warning before collapse, allowing for timely intervention and repair to prevent catastrophic failure.
Both are brittle or less predictable failure modes with limited ductility and high variability in construction quality.
The NSCP randomly assigns the same φ to unrelated failure modes, which can lead to inconsistencies in design safety margins.
Bearing and tied compression have the same nominal strength calculations, ensuring uniformity in design approach across different structural elements.

rationale.a: Both are relatively brittle (not ductile) compared to flexure.
rationale.c: Code provisions are based on structural behavior, not randomness.
rationale.d: The calculation methods differ; the φ factor reflects similar levels of predictability and ductility.
rationale.correct: Both bearing on concrete and tied column compression are relatively brittle. Bearing failure occurs suddenly when the bearing stress exceeds the local concrete strength; there is no gradual plastic deformation to warn the structure. Tied columns lack the ductility of spirally reinforced columns. Both receive φ = 0.70 because they are less forgiving.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: For shear and torsion failure modes, the NSCP strength reduction factor is:

rationale.d: φ = 0.90 applies to flexure and tension.

questions.text: A column in a residential building is designed as a tied column with dimensions 400 mm × 400 mm and reinforcement ratio ρ_g = 0.02. The nominal axial compression strength is P_n = 1200 kN. Using φ = 0.70, the design axial compression capacity is:

rationale.a: φ = 0.75 applies to spiral columns, not tied columns.
rationale.c: φ = 0.85 applies to shear and torsion.
rationale.d: φ = 0.90 applies to flexure and tension.
rationale.correct: The column is tied (not spiral), so φ = 0.70. Design capacity = 0.70(1200) = 840 kN. This is the maximum axial load the column can safely support.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: NSCP 2001, Section 4.2, Axial Compression Design and φ Factors

questions.text: A reinforced concrete beam is required to support a factored load that produces an internal moment. The nominal moment strength is M_n = 180 kN·m. Calculate the design moment capacity φM_n and determine if it is adequate for a required moment of 165 kN·m.

options.text: φMn = 0.85 × 180 = 153 kN·m; not adequate (153 < 165). The beam must be redesigned or reinforced to meet the required moment capacity.
φMn = 0.90 × 180 = 162 kN·m; not adequate (162 < 165). Additional reinforcement or a higher strength concrete mix may be necessary.
φMn = 0.90 × 180 = 162 kN·m; adequate if required is ≤162 kN·m; barely not adequate here.
φMn = 0.75 × 180 = 135 kN·m; not adequate (135 < 165). Consider increasing the beam depth or using a different reinforcement layout.

rationale.a: Shear uses φ = 0.85, not flexure. Also, even if correct, the calculation would yield 153 kN·m, which is not adequate.
rationale.b: The φ factor is correct, but the conclusion is wrong. 162 < 165, so NOT adequate.
rationale.d: Spiral compression uses φ = 0.75, not flexure.
rationale.correct: For flexure, φ = 0.90. Design capacity = 0.90(180) = 162 kN·m. Required capacity = 165 kN·m. Since 162 < 165, the section is not adequate; the beam must be redesigned with more reinforcement to increase M_n.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A design engineer is preparing a reinforced concrete column schedule. The column is specified with spiral reinforcement. Which φ factor should be used for axial compression design, and what is the engineering rationlea?

options.text: φ = 0.70; spiral and tied columns have the same reduction factor because they perform equally, which is incorrect
φ = 0.65 (tied), φ = 0.75 (spiral) for compression-controlled; spiral reinforcement provides continuous lateral confinement, allowing ductile behavior and higher capacity utilization.
φ = 0.85; spiral is as ductile as shear failure modes, which is not accurate
φ = 0.90; spiral reinforcement is as strong as flexural reinforcement, which is misleading

rationale.a: Spiral and tied columns perform differently; spiral provides better confinement.
rationale.c: Spiral is more ductile than shear modes but less ductile than flexure; φ = 0.85 is too high.
rationale.d: Flexure has the highest φ (0.90) because it is the most ductile. Spiral compression is less ductile.
rationale.correct: Spiral reinforcement consists of continuous helical hoops that confine the concrete core. This confinement increases ductility, allowing the column to redistribute load and deform visibly before collapse. The higher φ = 0.75 (compared to 0.70 for tied) recognizes this improved behavior.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.
